processing: Processed as sencha in every regional style, from light to deep steaming; single-cultivar lots are usually finished with a moderate firing to show the cultivar's balance.
harvest_season: Mid-season budding: first flush late April to mid-May depending on region, second flush in June–July.
appearance_dry: Classic dark green sencha needles, medium length, glossy.
appearance_liquor: Clear to lightly hazy bright yellow-green.
taste_profile: The reference sencha flavour: balanced grassy aroma, moderate umami, a clean sweetness and a firm but fair astringency that keeps it refreshing.

brewing.notes: Brew like standard sencha; it is the cultivar most brewing guides were written for. Hotter water (80 °C) brings more aroma at the cost of some astringency.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's first flush, usually as part of an unlabelled sencha (most sencha is Yabukita) or as a single-cultivar lot marked 'Yabukita' by farms that also sell Saemidori or Okumidori for comparison; shincha in spring, ichibancha through the year, and no ageing. The cultivar itself carries no price premium; region and grade set the price.
description:
Yabukita is the cultivar behind most Japanese tea. It was selected in 1908 by Sugiyama Hikosaburō from seedlings in a Shizuoka field, named for the plot on the north side of a cleared bamboo grove, registered as a cultivar in 1953 and planted so widely over the following decades that it came to cover about three-quarters of the country's tea fields. Its share is slipping now, but a bag of sencha with no cultivar on it is almost certainly Yabukita, and a single-cultivar lot labelled with the name is the reference point for everything else.

It won because it is a good all-rounder: cold-hardy, vigorous, high-yielding, mid-season in budding, and balanced in the cup in whatever style it is processed, from light-steamed mountain sencha to deep-steamed plateau tea, with a strong, fresh aroma and a frank astringency. The weaknesses are the ones of any monoculture: a harvest that lands on the same days everywhere, and susceptibility to disease, which is part of why newer cultivars such as Saemidori and Okumidori are gaining ground.

Brewed as standard sencha, 5 g for 150 ml at 75 °C for a minute, it gives the textbook profile: grassy and fresh with a moderate umami, a clean sweetness and a firm astringency that keeps it refreshing; it has more aroma and more grip than the sweet modern cultivars and less of their thickness. Hotter water brings up the aroma at the cost of bitterness. Most brewing guides for sencha were written with this cultivar in mind, so if a guide works for you, it probably works for Yabukita.

It is sold as the current year's first flush, either anonymously as ordinary sencha or as a labelled single-cultivar lot by farms that also offer their Saemidori or Okumidori for comparison; shincha in spring, then ichibancha through the year. Price depends on region and grade rather than on the cultivar, which carries no premium.

Use it as the baseline: drink a Yabukita from a given farm first, then its other cultivars, and the differences will be obvious.
sources_note: English Wikipedia title assumed to be 'Yabukita'; if absent, use 'Japanese tea' as umbrella. Selection year 1908 and registration 1953 are the usual dates given.
